Time Share Scam [6052]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Time Share

Two types of time share.
- Property ( time at a specific property same time every year - can convert time into points)
- Points ( can book holidays at resorts that have agreements with holiday clubs.)

Promises of time out and wonderful holidays that one ordinarily can’t afford.
Excellent sales pitches. Sign very lengthy agreements.

For some it works.

But then try and book holidays unable to get times that suit you. We have a case study who
Never went on a holiday. He has paid about R 15 000 to date.
Then levies start to increase yearly.

People get tired of not being able to get what they paid for and then want out of contract.
Only to find that contract is in perpetuity. ( Which according to our lawyer is a form of slavery.) Some time share companies want your offspring to continue with contract.

No-one will buy time share. Like mine.

We have pensioners who simply can’t afford it any longer but can’t get out of contract. Threatened by time share companies. Threatened with judgements. Not very friendly as initial presentation. Some will let you out of contract if you pay fee of over R 20 000.

We have a lawyer who for a fee will get you out of your contract. Trudie Broekmann

A group of people including V F Plus party who have about 900 people on their books went to National Consumer Commission about this in 2017. NCC found in the consumer’s favour and have made 6 recommendations. But have failed to implement it.

People are still struggling to get out of contracts.

Interviews

Lawyers

Case studies ( I have two – looking for a stronger case study.)
Werner Kempton Park – young couple paid R 15 000. Never been on holiday. Threatened by companies.
Diana Parys – similar. Had for 20 years and had 4 holidays. Not as emotional as I would have liked but very eloquent.

National Consumer Commissioner Ebrahim Mohamed said they have in the past two decades received thousands of complaints, particularly relating to the points system, perpetual contracts, unreasonable property levies and unavailability of accommodation that was not governed by the Consumer Protection Act.
Why nothing done.

Film presentations by holiday clubs and posing as potential clients.

VOASA – meant to be regulatory body but made up of holiday clubs and protect their own interests.

Confront with people trying to get out of contract.

Visuals – beautiful holiday images and their presentations.









Swindled holiday-makers have taken turns telling the National Consumer Commission's Timeshare Inquiry how they were bullied to sign perpetual contracts, paying holiday clubs thousands of rands for a share of holidays that never materialised.
Timeshare client Ebrahim Mayet told the first day of the hearings in Pretoria yesterday that he paid more than R50000 in holiday timeshares to two holiday clubs but all he got was a "fancy pen" and six holiday vouchers which proved impossible to redeem.
Timeshare is explained as a joint ownership of a holiday home, with subscribers gettting exclusive use of the property for a week depending on the points they have accumulated.
A subscriber pays a yearly membership fee and buys points which can be swapped for time at resorts, but Mayet said this was nothing but a scam. The Lenasia businessman first received a call from the travel clubs that told him he had won holidays but had to attend a presentation to redeem his prize.
At the presentations, said Mayet, he was told he could go to any holiday destinations listed on the brochure. He added that he was then pressured to sign a contract he never had a chance to read after he was made to believe it was a once-off opportunity.
In 2013, more than a year after paying deposits of R16000 and R7000 respectively as well as monthly payments of about R2000 to each of the two holiday clubs, he decided to redeem the points he had accumulated.
"I was told the holiday home was not available. I was then given several holiday vouchers to Thailand but to redeem them I needed to sit for three more presentations," Mayet said. "I realised that the points get you nothing. It is a scam. That is the bottom line.''
The 57-year-old tried to cancel the contract but was told it was perpetual and that his children would inherit it when he dies. "They wanted R23000 cancellation fee but I told them to go to hell."
Mayet said he ultimately stopped paying and was then threatened with blacklisting, but he told the two holiday clubs he couldn't care less.
Consumer commissioner Ebrahim Mohamed said they have in the past two decades received thousands of complaints, particularly relating to the points system, perpetual contracts, unreasonable property levies and unavailability of accommodation that was not governed by the Consumer Protection Act.
Mohamed said the commission has tried hard to help the consumers but the complaints never stopped. "It is this kind of behaviour by the vacation ownership industry that has prompted us to resort to a public inquiry to comprehensively deal with all consumer issues to find a permanent solution."

Timeshare Scam Script Edit 7c
V/O
Coping with the pace of life often leaves us breathless. We tell ourselves to somehow improve our work-life balance, and so we might fall for the promises that underlie the global timeshare industry – promises of a lifetime of affordable holidays for an upfront deposit and some annual management fees.
About three-quarters of a million South Africans own timeshare through one of about 9 big holiday timeshare companies here. They’re also called vacation clubs – and you either buy into fully furnished accommodation for one vacation spot a year. Or you can use the points system to buy points and redeem on different vacation spots.
Diana
And it just sounded absolutely wonderful that we would have at least 1 family holiday every year forever and ever.”
Sarah
“It was a dream come true that I could go on vacation with the kids and everything.”
V/O
Timeshare has been around for about four decades in South Africa and attracted customers who didn’t want to buy a holiday home or be saddled with unexpectedly big hotel bills but could co-own a place and some time in the sun.
Timeshare comes in two models - the first fractional ownership divides one property between multiple owners, giving you exclusive use of a property for a week or two a year. The second is a points system that works like a club where you pay an annual membership fee and buy points to redeem for nights at resorts.
But in the last few years growing discontent on consumer watchdogs have revealed deep flaws in the idea of timeshare.
Sarah
“So I was happy in the beginning I was going on those dream holidays until such time that I couldn’t make any more bookings and then it became a bit of a nightmare.”
Link
There are numerous vacation club memberships that operate on the point system and many people have made use of this service and enjoyed their holidays, but when searching online there are hundreds of dissatisfied customers. I mean look at this one, capital letters, AVOID, AVOID, AVOID.
VO
What more and more timeshare members are discovering are the flaws inherent in the system - they struggle to find resort space; the marketing is often misleading and the lifetime contracts are overly complex. Nonetheless, the dream is still being sold.


Businesswoman Sarah Smith wanted to invest in quality family-time and bought into the point system. She paid R69 000 in 2006 which she paid off over 7 years and she also had to pay the monthly administration fee for the rest of her life.
Sarah
So I am paying like R 1000 a month and I can’t get any bookings and I paid all of this money, so when I tried to complain numerous emails, no response, kept on getting more and more frustrated thereafter.
V/O
When adding it up Sarah Smith has paid about R 150 000 for a handful of local holidays.
Diana Delmont who also bought on the point system 17 years ago faced similarly large expenses.
Diana
We spent over the time we spent R 118 000 and for that we got 4 very mediocre holidays.
V/O
Posing as a buyer Carte Blanche wanted to know whether the small army of timeshare salespeople out there warn customers of the risks. We call our salesman Fred - he’s been selling timeshare for 19 years and threw in a free holiday to sweeten the deal.
Fred
Should you decide to take this I will give you a free week for 8 people.
V/O
We discovered that Fred is well aware of the problems of the point system - he says he doesn’t sell them anymore but encouraged us to go for the fractional ownership model rather. Points, he said, have been a problem.
Fred
I had a client the other day She had 107 points and was paying R 17000 a year, which is a lot of money and she can’t get availability.
And the other thing is she is stuck in that thing for the rest of her life.
V/O
With salespeople still signing customers up, trying to get over 750 000 people booked into fewer than 200 local resorts means owners like Diana Delmont and Sarah Smith couldn’t book holidays.
But when they tried to cancel their contracts, they discovered the second big problem with the concept - their contracts are for life. The timeshare company would not release them from the agreements.
Attorney Trudie Broekmann specialises in consumer law and now also timeshare issues.
Masa
You have also referred to these contracts as some for of slavery?
Trudie
“Yes, the contracts are contracts in perpetuity, in other words they have a duration until you die. These are valid contracts in South Africa. But in the European Union they are not valid so if you are bound by a contract and you have to pay, pay, pay until you die and there is no way of getting out that is a type of slavery and you are bound by that thing.”
V/O
When Sarah Smith tried to sell her points, she discovered that no one wanted them.
Masa
“How did you wiggle your way out of the contract?”
Sarah
“I haven’t wiggled my way out, I am still obliged to them.
V/O
Broekmann was able to cancel the onerous contracts for over 550 unhappy timeshare clients, relying on the provisions of the Consumer Protection Act and other law.
Trudie
We have discovered that most of the timeshare contracts are actually invalid because they don’t comply with the relevant laws or there was such serious misrepresentation right at the start of the contract, so no body every tells you that you are going to be bound by this contract until you die. And then sometimes they even try and make your heirs take over the contract.
V/O
The idea of her heirs taking on this burden cast a dark shadow on Diana Delmont’s life
Diana
I would say I felt in bondage, I was definitely in bondage and I felt like I had a millstone around my neck from the bloody payments every single month
V/O
Trudie Broekmann was able to cancel Delmont’s contract.
But these are not isolated cases. When timeshare companies did not respond to their members’ pleas, the National Consumer Commission or NCC intervened.
Link
For over 2 decades the NCC was inundated with complaints from consumers about their timeshare points, which lead to an enquiry into the industry in 2017 and in the final report it found that and I quote “The NCC has always held the view that the complaints from the timeshare consumers are valid and warranted.”
V/O
Prudence Moilwa heads up the NCC’s Enforcement and Investigations.
Prudence
At the end of the day after understanding we know for sure that what you are doing is not above board and that is why we then said to them cancellation of contracts where consumers making allegations of heavy handed marketing and misrepresentation, we agreed with them at that point they will be cancelled and they should be cancelled.
V/O
The NCC received 1300 complaints from people who couldn’t get out of their contracts - the NCC commission saw to it that all of these contracts were cancelled and those matters have been resolved.
Masa
And during the enquiry what kinds of stories were you hearing?”
Prudence
“You know we heard horrific stories from consumers , of situations where people literally were saying they were near committing suicide. We are dealing with an industry that does not have compassion.
V/O
In our investigation, we asked salesman Fred repeatedly for a copy of the contract before we would sign up - especially the cancellation clause, Fred said the company would not send it without us paying an upfront deposit.
Fred
We can’t do it, its with the new law, we are not allowed to send any blank contracts to any client, because anything can happen.
Are you saying that I have to pay some money before I can actually see this contract.
Because for the developer to release the week, yes.”


V/O
Jannie Smuts works in construction and he’s desperately trying to get out of a 15 year fractional ownership contract he signed just 7 months ago. He met with unforseen business challenges. The time share company however wants a R9970 cancellation fee - he simply doesn’t have it.
Masa
“So you are stuck?”
Jannie
“I’m stuck, stuck with them. I did ask them they can keep the money I already paid.
Masa
“So you are willing for them to keep the money that you have been paying and the initial deposit even though you never went on holiday?”
Jannie
“Yes.”
V/O
The Vacation Ownership Association of Southern Africa or VOASA is a voluntary industry body that represents most timeshare companies - and it declined an interview with Carte Blanche.
In a written statement the body defended its position that “Based on legal advice and a long-standing cost recovery principle” it was legal to charge cancellation fees.
It said that timeshare companies have responsibilities…
Timeshare owners have certain rights in terms of their ownership and incur certain duties, including the duty to contribute annually to the levy fund.
Masa
“If you had the opportunity to speak to the representatives. What would you say to them?”
Jannie
“They must explain to me a few things. How can you be unhuman when somebody can’t afford something anymore and he didn’t even benefit from it. They are the only ones that really benefiting from it.”
Prudence
“But where a consumer has not used the product at all and all they have is the contract with your company consumers should be allowed to get out of this contract.”
Masa
“The reason they gave him is that he would be a burden to other members if he eliminates his membership so they need his money to fund other people’s holidays.”
Prudence
“The argument of the club and other membership did not hold water, because there is no point of saturation. There is no point where they now say we have enough members then it is impossible for them to make an argument that when you leave other members will suffer. So that is why we came to a point of saying consumers should have the right to cancel. “
V/O
Trudie Broekmann believes that customers don’t need the consent of timeshare companies to cancel their contracts.
Trudie
“If you cancel based on legal grounds then consent to cancellation is not a requirement, if you have a legal right to cancel then exercise the cancellation in the cancellation letter and then the response is not actually relevant. The contract is legally cancelled no further fees need to be paid and that is the end of the story.”
Masa
How do you feel now?
Jannie
Angry
I made a huge mistake by signing up for something like this and I would like actually to warn other people to think very clearly before they sign something like this.
V/O
The NCC says that the Department of Trade and Industry is working on provisions
that will soon kick in to bring order to the industry once and for all.
Prudence
Our warning from the commission side is to say that we will come after you and make sure you comply with the law.



Promo 11 secs
It’s legal here, but in Europe it’s seen as a form of slavery. Many timeshare members don’t know that their contract is for life.
And like slaves in the past, you have to pay to buy your freedom.

Promo 21 secs
How does the timeshare industry get 750 000 members accommodation in under 200 resorts. For many they don’t. After paying tens of thousands of rands for a lifetime of holidays, dissatisfied timeshare members who can’t get accommodation find out when they want to cancel their agreement that they have signed for life.
Promo 21 Secs

The Timeshare/Vacation Club Industry finds itself on a slippery slope
“We know that what you are doing is not above board.”
A timeshare club insisted a new member, who fell on hard times, would have to pay to cancel his contract.
“How can they be so inhuman, the only people who benefit is themselves.’

He met with unforseen business challenges. The time share company however wants a R9970 cancellation fee - he simply doesn’t have it. Masa “So you are stuck?” Jannie “I’m stuck, stuck with them. I did ask them they can keep the money I already paid. Masa “So you are willing for them to keep the money that you have been paying and the initial deposit even though you never went on holiday?” Jannie “Yes.” V/O The Vacation Ownership Association of Southern Africa or VOASA is a voluntary industry body that represents most timeshare companies - and it declined an interview with Carte Blanche. In a written statement the body defended its position that “Based on legal advice and a long-standing cost recovery principle” it was legal to charge cancellation fees. It said that timeshare companies have responsibilities… Timeshare owners have certain rights in terms of their ownership and incur certain duties, including the duty to contribute annually to the levy fund. Masa “If you had the opportunity to speak to the representatives. What would you say to them?” Jannie “They must explain to me a few things. How can you be unhuman when somebody can’t afford something anymore and he didn’t even benefit from it. They are the only ones that really benefiting from it.” Prudence “But where a consumer has not used the product at all and all they have is the contract with your company consumers should be allowed to get out of this contract.” Masa “The reason they gave him is that he would be a burden to other members if he eliminates his membership so they need his money to fund other people’s holidays.” Prudence “The argument of the club and other membership did not hold water, because there is no point of saturation. There is no point where they now say we have enough members then it is impossible for them to make an argument that when you leave other members will suffer. So that is why we came to a point of saying consumers should have the right to cancel. “ V/O Trudie Broekmann believes that customers don’t need the consent of timeshare companies to cancel their contracts. Trudie “If you cancel based on legal grounds then consent to cancellation is not a requirement, if you have a legal right to cancel then exercise the cancellation in the cancellation letter and then the response is not actually relevant. The contract is legally cancelled no further fees need to be paid and that is the end of the story.” Masa How do you feel now? Jannie Angry I made a huge mistake by signing up for something like this and I would like actually to warn other people to think very clearly before they sign something like this. V/O The NCC says that the Department of Trade and Industry is working on provisions that will soon kick in to bring order to the industry once and for all. Prudence Our warning from the commission side is to say that we will come after you and make sure you comply with the law. Promo 11 secs It’s legal here, but in Europe it’s seen as a form of slavery. Many timeshare members don’t know that their contract is for life. And like slaves in the past, you have to pay to buy your freedom. Promo 21 secs How does the timeshare industry get 750 000 members accommodation in under 200 resorts. For many they don’t. After paying tens of thousands of rands for a lifetime of holidays, dissatisfied timeshare members who can’t get accommodation find out when they want to cancel their agreement that they have signed for life. Promo 21 Secs The Timeshare/Vacation Club Industry finds itself on a slippery slope “We know that what you are doing is not above board.” A timeshare club insisted a new member, who fell on hard times, would have to pay to cancel his contract. “How can they be so inhuman, the only people who benefit is themselves.’

metadata.Further information: Time Share Two types of time share. - Property ( time at a specific property same time every year - can convert time into points) - Points ( can book holidays at resorts that have agreements with holiday clubs.) Promises of time out and wonderful holidays that one ordinarily can’t afford. Excellent sales pitches. Sign very lengthy agreements. For some it works. But then try and book holidays unable to get times that suit you. We have a case study who Never went on a holiday. He has paid about R 15 000 to date. Then levies start to increase yearly. People get tired of not being able to get what they paid for and then want out of contract. Only to find that contract is in perpetuity. ( Which according to our lawyer is a form of slavery.) Some time share companies want your offspring to continue with contract. No-one will buy time share. Like mine. We have pensioners who simply can’t afford it any longer but can’t get out of contract. Threatened by time share companies. Threatened with judgements. Not very friendly as initial presentation. Some will let you out of contract if you pay fee of over R 20 000. We have a lawyer who for a fee will get you out of your contract. Trudie Broekmann A group of people including V F Plus party who have about 900 people on their books went to National Consumer Commission about this in 2017. NCC found in the consumer’s favour and have made 6 recommendations. But have failed to implement it. People are still struggling to get out of contracts. Interviews Lawyers Case studies ( I have two – looking for a stronger case study.) Werner Kempton Park – young couple paid R 15 000. Never been on holiday. Threatened by companies. Diana Parys – similar. Had for 20 years and had 4 holidays. Not as emotional as I would have liked but very eloquent. National Consumer Commissioner Ebrahim Mohamed said they have in the past two decades received thousands of complaints, particularly relating to the points system, perpetual contracts, unreasonable property levies and unavailability of accommodation that was not governed by the Consumer Protection Act. Why nothing done. Film presentations by holiday clubs and posing as potential clients. VOASA – meant to be regulatory body but made up of holiday clubs and protect their own interests. Confront with people trying to get out of contract. Visuals – beautiful holiday images and their presentations. Swindled holiday-makers have taken turns telling the National Consumer Commission's Timeshare Inquiry how they were bullied to sign perpetual contracts, paying holiday clubs thousands of rands for a share of holidays that never materialised. Timeshare client Ebrahim Mayet told the first day of the hearings in Pretoria yesterday that he paid more than R50000 in holiday timeshares to two holiday clubs but all he got was a "fancy pen" and six holiday vouchers which proved impossible to redeem. Timeshare is explained as a joint ownership of a holiday home, with subscribers gettting exclusive use of the property for a week depending on the points they have accumulated. A subscriber pays a yearly membership fee and buys points which can be swapped for time at resorts, but Mayet said this was nothing but a scam. The Lenasia businessman first received a call from the travel clubs that told him he had won holidays but had to attend a presentation to redeem his prize. At the presentations, said Mayet, he was told he could go to any holiday destinations listed on the brochure. He added that he was then pressured to sign a contract he never had a chance to read after he was made to believe it was a once-off opportunity. In 2013, more than a year after paying deposits of R16000 and R7000 respectively as well as monthly payments of about R2000 to each of the two holiday clubs, he decided to redeem the points he had accumulated. "I was told the holiday home was not available. I was then given several holiday vouchers to Thailand but to redeem them I needed to sit for three more presentations," Mayet said. "I realised that the points get you nothing. It is a scam. That is the bottom line.'' The 57-year-old tried to cancel the contract but was told it was perpetual and that his children would inherit it when he dies. "They wanted R23000 cancellation fee but I told them to go to hell." Mayet said he ultimately stopped paying and was then threatened with blacklisting, but he told the two holiday clubs he couldn't care less. Consumer commissioner Ebrahim Mohamed said they have in the past two decades received thousands of complaints, particularly relating to the points system, perpetual contracts, unreasonable property levies and unavailability of accommodation that was not governed by the Consumer Protection Act. Mohamed said the commission has tried hard to help the consumers but the complaints never stopped. "It is this kind of behaviour by the vacation ownership industry that has prompted us to resort to a public inquiry to comprehensively deal with all consumer issues to find a permanent solution."
